label: Starship Integrated Flight Tests
delta: UPDATE (Sep 17): SpaceX announced Flight 14 has slipped again, from Sept 22 to no earlier than Sept 28, 2026 (75-minute window still opening 7:15am CT/8:15am EDT from Starbase) — the fourth target change, with no reason disclosed. Booster 21 and Ship 41 remain in final Starbase checkout after completing their static-fire campaigns (B21's 33-engine test Aug 28; Ship 41's six-engine test Aug 21). Previously (Sep 14): NASASpaceflight reported Flight 14's target had slipped from the previously reported Sept 18 window to no earlier than Sept 22, 2026 — the third target change in as many weeks, with no vehicle problem disclosed. During the gap, SpaceX moved next-generation Ship 42 to Pad 2's tower Sept 12 and rehearsed chopstick lateral-translation and Quick Disconnect reconnection ahead of Flight 15's planned first catch attempt. Flight 14 remains SpaceX's first bid at full orbital insertion (~6 orbits, ~275km altitude, ~10 hours, Pacific splashdown west of Chile), carrying roughly 20-26 operational Starlink V3 satellites (source counts vary). Prior: an FAA Space Operations Advisory reported Sept 11 set the launch window for Sept 18, 2026 (12:15-14:14 UTC, Sept 19 backup) from Starbase — a few days later than the Sept 15 no-earlier-than date SpaceX had cited in its Aug 31 FCC filing; SpaceX had not officially confirmed Flight 14 as of Sept 12. The FAA has already issued a Finding of No Significant Impact and Record of Decision for the flight; the outstanding item is FCC Special Temporary Authority (filed Aug 31, requested approval by Sept 15) to transmit with the ~20 Starlink V3 satellites aboard. Speaking Sept 10 at Goldman Sachs' Communacopia and Technology Conference, CFO Bret Johnsen said Flight 14 would be Starship's first revenue-generating flight. Separately, the next Starship pairing (Ship 42 / Booster 22, for a future Flight 15) began testing at Massey's test site. Prior status: as of Sept 7, both Flight 14 vehicles had finished their required single-vehicle tests and were in final checkout — Ship 41 in Mega Bay 2, Booster 21 in Mega Bay 1, with Flight Termination System placards now visible on both bays. Next steps are loading the Starlink V3 payload into Ship 41, then rolling the booster and ship out for stacking; the current no-earlier-than date is still Sept 15, 2026, per CADENA/COMPASS Space Operations planning slides, though SpaceX has not made that an official target. An Aug 31 FCC filing requesting Starlink V3 spectrum authorization set Sept 15 as the target launch/deployment date — the first filing to put a full orbital-insertion profile on Flight 14's paperwork, confirming Musk's Aug 4 earnings-call comment that the flight would carry next-generation V3 satellites (~20 units, ~1 Tbps downlink each) into an operational orbit rather than the short suborbital arcs flown since IFT-6. On Sept 3-4, the FAA issued a Finding of No Significant Impact on its Final Tiered Environmental Assessment for expanded Starship reentry/landing options — a new Northern Pacific contingency area plus expanded Hawaii/Central Pacific and Southeast Pacific contingency zones — giving SpaceX backup splashdown options if the Boca Chica return path or catch tower can't be used; the primary recovery plan for Ship 41 remains an Indian Ocean splashdown, per Musk's Aug 20 comment that a tower catch of the ship is still 'a few months' out rather than on Flight 14. Separately, next-generation Ship 42 rolled out to Massey's Test Site and completed a pair of cryogenic proof tests (methane and LOX header tanks) late Sept 3, clearing it to return to Mega Bay 2 for engine installation ahead of a later flight. Hardware status leading into checkout: Booster 21 completed a full 33-engine static fire at Pad 2 Aug 28, and underwent a chopsticks lift-and-catch rehearsal on the launch tower Aug 29; Ship 41 completed single-engine (Aug 19) and six-engine (Aug 21) static fires at Massey's Test Site. IFT-13 (Booster 20 V3 + Ship 40 V3) completed July 24, 2026 after a July 16 T-0 abort (6 Raptors flagged low LOX turbopump pressure from moisture; 2 engines replaced before reflight). Results: first-ever deployment of operational satellites — 20 V3 Starlink sats (6 with cameras) released in suborbit and contacted ground stations; Ship 40 relit all 3 Raptors and made a soft Indian Ocean splashdown, remaining intact afterward for the first close-up post-flight heat-shield inspection. Booster 20 was lost on its Gulf of Mexico splashdown attempt — only 10 of 13 landing-burn engines relit, 5 shut down seconds later, causing a hard impact. Prior: FAA cleared Starship to resume flights July 13, 2026, closing the IFT-12 mishap investigation (heat effects on propulsion + erroneous engine alarm settings that prevented Booster 19's reignition, May 22 loss).
